::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives

- Draw a pipeline's rule graph and job graph, and read what is done and what is pending.
- Write a pytest test that dry-runs the pipeline and checks job counts worked out from the samplesheet.
- Run those tests on every push with GitHub Actions.
- Read `snakemake --lint` output and decide which findings matter.
- Pin what a rerun next year needs, and keep a record of what ran.

Time: 35 min
:::

## What you can check without running anything

A dry run reads the samplesheet and the config, builds every job, checks that
every input file exists, and stops. It takes seconds and needs no tools and no
conda environments. Most bugs in a pipeline are wiring bugs: a switch that
pulls in the wrong rules, a control matched to the wrong sample, a typo in a
path. A dry run catches all of those.

What it cannot catch: a wrong flag to `macs3`, a tool that crashes, a script
with a bug. For those you need a real run on small data. On the course data, a
full RegPipe run takes a few minutes once the conda envs exist.

## The rule graph

```bash
snakemake --rulegraph -s workflows/RegPipe.snakefile --cores 1 | dot -Tsvg > rulegraph.svg
```

{{< generated name="regpipe-rulegraph" alt="RegPipe rule graph: one box per rule, arrows from each rule to the rules that use its outputs" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
One box per rule, an arrow where one rule's output is another's input. This
is the picture to put in a README. `--dag` draws one box per *job* instead: 61
boxes for RegPipe, useful to check that each ChIP sample points at its own
control, unreadable for a pipeline with hundreds of samples. TTpipe keeps its
rule graph in the docs and has a test that fails when the picture is out of
date ([Rule graph](../field-guide/ttpipe.qmd#tt-rulegraph)).

`dot` comes from Graphviz, which is in the course env (`envs/course.yml`).
:::

## What is done, what is pending: `--summary`

`--summary` lists every output file with its rule, date and status. Here, after
making one filtered BAM, with `minMapq` changed to 20:

{{< generated name="regpipe-summary-changed" command="false" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Read the `status` column: `missing` (never made), `ok`, `removed temp file`
(the `temp()` aligned BAM), and `params changed`. The command was:

```bash
snakemake --summary -s workflows/RegPipe.snakefile --cores 1 --config minMapq=20
```

It is long, one row per file. Pipe it through `grep` or open it in a
spreadsheet.
:::

## `--list-changes` in 8.27.1

`snakemake --list-changes params` should print the output files whose params
changed. In Snakemake 8.27.1 it crashes, before it looks at any file:

{{< generated name="regpipe-list-changes" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`--list-changes code` fails too, with a different `TypeError`;
`--list-changes input` works. The bug was fixed in Snakemake 9.5.0. Until the
lab pipelines move to 9, use the `status` column of `--summary` above, or the
`reason:` lines of a dry run (module 7), to see what changed.
:::

## A dry-run test

`tests/test_dryrun.py` runs Snakemake with `-n` and checks the job counts. The
expected counts are not typed in. They are worked out from the samplesheet,
the same way the workflow does it:

{{< snippet repo="regpipe" file="tests/test_dryrun.py" def="expected_jobs" >}}

## Running the dry run from a test

{{< snippet repo="regpipe" file="tests/test_dryrun.py" def="dry_run" >}}

{{< snippet repo="regpipe" file="tests/test_dryrun.py" def="test_dry_run_job_counts" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`job_counts()` (in the same file) reads the `Job stats` table that a dry run
prints. Two details make the test trustworthy:

- `outputDir={tmp_path}` sends the dry run to an empty folder, so every job is
  listed even if you have a finished run in `output/`.
- `expected_jobs()` reads the samplesheet with `keep_default_na=False`, like
  `common.smk`. Without it, pandas reads the `Control` value `NA` as missing,
  the controls are counted wrong, and the test fails for a reason that has
  nothing to do with the workflow.

If you add two samples to the samplesheet, the test still passes, because the
expected counts move with it. A test that asserts `total == 61` would fail and
teach you nothing.
:::

## Run the tests

```bash
cd course-pipeline
python -m pytest tests/
```

{{< generated name="regpipe-pytest" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Four tests: the job counts, that each ChIP's `macs3` command names its own
control and DNase gets none, the counts with `scatter_chunks=3`, and that a
`Control` naming no sample stops the run before anything starts. They skip
themselves when Snakemake or the course data are missing, so a `pytest` on a
machine without them reports skips rather than failures.
:::

## How TTpipe tests its switches

TTpipe has more switches, so most of its tests are about job-count differences:

{{< snippet repo="ttpipe" file="tests/test_dryrun.py" lines="50-60" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
TTpipe does not ship real data in its repository, so its tests run against
placeholder files in `tests/dryrun/` and a config that points at them. A dry
run only checks that files exist, so placeholders are enough. RegPipe can use
the real course data instead, because the course repository carries a 39 MB
subset. The field guide compares this with the community's `.test/` folders in
[Tests](../field-guide/conventions.qmd#tests).
:::

## CI: run the tests on every push

TTpipe runs its tests on GitHub Actions for every push and pull request:

{{< snippet repo="ttpipe" file=".github/workflows/ci.yml" lang="yaml" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
No conda, no tools, no data: Snakemake from `config/requirements.txt` and
pytest. It tells you, on the pull request page, whether the change broke the
wiring. `bash -n` checks that the
launcher scripts at least parse. MicroCPipe has the same workflow
([tests](../field-guide/microcpipe.qmd#mc-tests)).
:::

## `snakemake --lint`

The linter reads the workflow and suggests style fixes. On RegPipe:

{{< generated name="regpipe-lint" lines="1-14" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
The full output is about 960 lines. We counted the findings: 156, of two kinds,
85 "absolute path" and 71 "path composition with `+`". Both come from the same
habit, `OUT + "/{sample}/..."`. `OUT` comes from the config, so nothing is
really hard-coded, but the linter cannot know that. There are no rule-level
findings: every rule has a `log:`, no shell command uses a variable from
outside the rule, and there is no `run:` block.

The field guide has the same analysis for the three lab pipelines, with what
each finding means for lab style: see
[What `snakemake --lint` says](../field-guide/conventions.qmd#lint).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .exercise}

## Pin what a rerun needs

Someone reruns your analysis in a year. What has to be the same?

| What | Where RegPipe pins it |
|---|---|
| Snakemake | `config/requirements.txt`: `snakemake==8.27.1` |
| Tools | `envs/*.yml`: `bowtie2=2.5.5`, `samtools=1.24`, ... |
| Channels | `envs/*.yml`: conda-forge, bioconda, `nodefaults` |
| Pipeline code | the git commit |
| Settings | `config/RegConfig.yaml` and the samplesheet |
| Reference data | `data/README.md`: ENCODE and GEO accessions |

{{< snippet repo="regpipe" file="envs/regpipe_align.yml" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
One gap: `snakemake-executor-plugin-slurm>=1.0` has no upper bound, so a new
install gets the newest plugin that pip finds. The container this course was
built in has 2.8.0. If a cluster run breaks after a fresh install, pin the
plugin to the version that worked.

Snakemake also warns on every run that conda is not set to strict channel
priority. Set it once with `conda config --set channel_priority strict`; the
env files assume it.
:::

## Keep a record of what ran

Each run leaves a record. Keep it with the results:

- `.snakemake/log/<date>.snakemake.log`: every job, its command and its result.
- `output/logs/<rule>/`: each tool's own messages.
- `output/benchmarks/<rule>/`: time and memory per job.
- `snakemake --summary`: every output with the rule and the date that made it.
- The commit you ran: `git rev-parse --short HEAD`, in your notebook entry.

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Snakemake does not record the git commit for you. The simplest habit is to
commit before a real run and write the short hash next to the results. The
`onstart` hook from module 6 is a good place to print it if you want it in the
log automatically.
:::

## Stopping point D

This is RegPipe as it ships in `course-pipeline/`: the lab layout, switches,
scatter-gather, `directory()` for the index, and dry-run tests. If you fell
behind, copy `stopping-points/stopD/` (the same pipeline, with `dataDir` set
for its folder) and check it:

```bash
cp -r stopping-points/stopD my-regpipe
cd my-regpipe
bash RegPipe.sh -n          # 61 jobs
python -m pytest tests/     # 4 passed
```

This is where the two workshop days end.

## What next

Two ways to keep going:

- [Snakemake-ify](../exercises/snakemakeify.qmd): ten old lab scripts to turn
  into rules, one at a time, ending with a whole `run_all.sh` as one Snakefile.
  Each one practices something from modules 1-8.
- [The capstone](../capstone.qmd): take an analysis you actually run and turn
  it into a pipeline in the lab layout, with a launcher, profiles and a dry-run
  test. You pair up with someone and review each other's.

Pick your capstone analysis before you leave today, and find a partner.

## Key points

- A dry run is a test of the wiring. It takes seconds and needs no tools or data beyond the inputs existing.
- Work out expected job counts from the samplesheet in the test, so the test survives new samples.
- `--rulegraph` for the README, `--dag` to check one sample's wiring, `--summary` for what is done.
- In 8.27.1, `--list-changes params` crashes; use `--summary` or dry-run reasons.
- Run the tests in CI on every push; `bash -n` the launchers too.
- Most `--lint` findings in lab pipelines are about `+` path building. They are style, not bugs.
- Pin Snakemake, the tools and the plugin, and write down the commit you ran.
